\chapter{Introduction}
Fatigue cracking limits the service life of welded joints in
steel bridges, and assessment methods must balance conservatism
against the cost of unnecessary strengthening.
This interim report reviews the two assessment families used in
our current practice and presents the first round of parametric
crack-growth calculations.

\section{Assessment Families}
Stress-life approaches use nominal stress ranges from design
codes together with classified detail categories.
Fracture mechanics approaches instead track the growth of an
initial flaw under the service stress spectrum and predict the
number of cycles needed to reach a critical crack size.

\section{Baseline Integration Script}
The crack-growth integration is performed with a short Python
driver that steps the Paris law forward block by block over the
service spectrum. The core loop is reproduced below for reference:

\begin{verbatim}
for block in spectrum:
    dK = delta_K(a, block.stress_range)
    if dK > dK_th:
        a += C * dK**m * block.cycles
        if a >= a_crit:
            break

\chapter{Results}
The threshold stress intensity range dK_th was taken from the
material qualification tests reported in the previous phase.
Across all twenty-four welded details, the predicted cycles to
a_crit scatter within a factor of two of the measured test lives.
The Paris exponent m = 3.1 gives the best overall agreement,
while the coefficient C = 1.8e-13 keeps the predictions on the
conservative side for the as-welded specimens.
Predictions for the T_joints are the least accurate, because the
local weld geometry deviates most from the assumed ideal profile.

\chapter{Results}
The threshold stress intensity range $\Delta K_{th}$ was taken from the
material qualification tests reported in the previous phase.
Across all twenty-four welded details, the predicted cycles to
$a_{crit}$ scatter within a factor of two of the measured test lives.
The Paris exponent $m = 3.1$ gives the best overall agreement,
while the coefficient $C = 1.8 \times 10^{-13}$ keeps the predictions on the
conservative side for the as-welded specimens.
Predictions for the T-joints are the least accurate, because the
local weld geometry deviates most from the assumed ideal profile.
